h1: Funding whisky that cannot be sold for years
title: Funding Whisky That Cannot Be Sold Yet | Craft Beer School
desc: How craft distilleries fund years of maturing whisky stock: the cash gap, the usual funding routes and how to plan for them.
teaser: Every cask you fill is cash you will not see for years. The distilleries that survive plan the wait before they fill the first one.
standfirst: A whisky distillery spends money today on stock it can sell years from now. That gap breaks more craft distilleries than bad spirit does. Here is how to size the gap and the routes founders use to fund it.
sections: The cash gap is the business model

A brewery can sell beer a few weeks after brewing it. A whisky distillery cannot. Scotch must spend at least three years in oak. Many premium releases are much older. Even where local rules allow younger spirit, quality whisky usually needs years in the cask.

During those years you pay for grain, energy, labour, casks, warehouse space, insurance and excise compliance. You also lose spirit to evaporation, which in Indian heat runs well above the roughly 2% a year often quoted for Scotland. The cost of every litre rises while it waits. None of it comes back until the first bottle sells.
Size the gap with your own numbers

Build a simple model before you talk to any funder. For each year, list the litres of pure alcohol (LPA) you will fill, the cost to make each LPA, the cask cost per LPA and the yearly warehouse cost. Then apply your expected loss each year.

Here is the shape of the working. Fill 50,000 LPA in year one. If you lose 5% of the remaining volume each year, about 42,900 LPA is left after three years and about 40,700 after four. Every year you also fill another batch. By the first release, you are carrying three or four years of production at once. The money tied up in that stock is your funding requirement, before you count the building and the stills.

Use your measured loss rate once you have one. Until then, test a range of rates and see how much the funding need moves.

Most craft distilleries start with founders' money and equity investors. Investors in whisky need patience. They also need to understand that returns come late. A clear plan showing when revenue starts, from which products, makes that conversation easier.

Be careful with promises. Whisky values are not guaranteed to rise. Stock can be lost to leaks, quality problems or fire. Any investor document should be prepared with legal and financial advisers, not built from a spreadsheet alone.

Banks will often lend against land, buildings and equipment. Lending against maturing whisky stock is harder for a new distillery, because the stock has no sales history and no proven value. Established whisky companies do borrow against inventory, but they have years of records behind them.

So expect bank debt to fund part of the capital cost, not the stock. Plan the stock funding from equity, early revenue or both.

The common routes to early revenue are:

  • Unaged spirits. Gin and other white spirits can be sold within weeks. Our guide to what a new distillery sells while whisky ages covers the options.
  • Contract distilling. Making new make or spirit for other brands uses spare still time.
  • Cask programmes. Selling casks to private buyers brings cash in early, but it brings legal, excise and reputational questions with it.
  • Visitor income. Tours and a shop, where state rules allow, bring in modest steady revenue.
  • Sourced whisky. Some new brands bottle whisky from another distillery under their own label while their own stock matures, with honest labelling.

Funding is easier when the release plan is clear. Decide which casks are earmarked for a first release, which for older expressions and which for a core range. Selling everything at the earliest age brings cash sooner but leaves no older stock for later. Holding too much back starves the business. Our guide to whisky inventory planning goes into the balance.

A yearly model shows the size of the gap. A monthly model shows when you run out of money. Build one for the first five years at least. Put grain, energy, wages, cask purchases and warehouse costs in the months they are paid, not averaged across the year. Casks often arrive in large shipments that need paying for up front. Licence renewals and insurance renew on fixed dates.

Then add revenue in the months it really arrives. Gin sales in India often take time to collect, because distributors and state corporations pay on their own terms. A sale booked in March may turn into cash months later.

The lowest point on the monthly cash line is the number your funding must cover, with a margin on top. Most founders find it is later and deeper than their yearly model suggested.

If you are planning a distillery, build the stock model this week: fills per year, cost per LPA, loss rate and release ages. It will tell you how much funding the wait needs. Then learn the process well enough that every cost line in it is a number you can defend.
faqs: Why is whisky hard to fund?
Spirit must mature for years before it can be sold as whisky, so a distillery pays to make and store stock long before any revenue comes back.
Will a bank lend against maturing whisky?
Banks usually lend against land and equipment first. Lending against maturing stock is harder for a new distillery with no sales history.
How do craft distilleries earn money before their whisky is ready?
Common routes are gin and other unaged spirits, contract distilling, visitor income and carefully run cask programmes.
